blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Structural isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different connectivity of atoms, resulting in distinct structures and properties.

blocks.title: Key Points: Types of Structural Isomers
blocks.text:
Chain Isomerism(C.I.)

  • Definition: Isomers differ in the carbon chain (straight vs. branched).
  • Example:
Position Isomerism (P.I.)

  • Definition: Isomers differ in the position of a functional group, substituent, or double/triple bond.
  • Example
Functional Group Isomerism(F.G.I.)

  • Definition: Compounds which have the same molecular formula but different functional groups are functional group isomers.
  • Example:
Metamerism

  • Definition: Compounds which have the same molecular formula, and the same functional group but different alkyl groups attached to a polyvalent functional group
  • Example

blocks.title: Degree of Unsaturation / Double Bond Equivalent/ Index of Hydrogen Deficiency
blocks.text:
D.U/D.B.E./I.H.D. = No. of π bond + No. of rings

If D.U. = 0 (Νο π bond/ring)

D.U. = 1 (1 π bond/1 ring)

D.U. = 2 (2 π bonds/2 rings/1 π bond + 1 ring/1 triple bond)

blocks.title: Number of Structural Isomers
blocks.text:
The number of structural isomers possible for $C_4H_{10}O$  is 7.

$C_4H_{10}O$  D.U= 0 (no π bond), so only alcohols and ethers are formed.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Consider the given set of compounds: pentane, butane, 2-methyl butane, and propane. The number of pairs of isomers possible will be_____.

A. 1
B. 2
C. 4
D. 3
blocks.answer:
Answer: A

Solution: Chemical compounds with identical formulas but different physical or chemical properties are named isomers. Therefore, only pentane and 2-methyl butane can show isomerism because they have the same chemical formula $C_5H_{12}$ and the number of possible pairs is equal to 1.

So, option A is the correct answer.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Which of the following pairs are structural isomers?

(a) $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$and $\text{CH}_3\text{OCH}_3$
(b) $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$
(c)$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$
(d) $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3$
blocks.answer:
Ans. (a) $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$and $\text{CH}_3\text{OCH}_3$

Explanation: These compounds have the same molecular formula  but different structures

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing functional group isomers with chain or position isomers.
  • Missing possible isomers due to incomplete visualization of structures.
  • Ignoring IUPAC naming rules for correct identification.
  • Overlooking stereoisomerism differences.

blocks.title: Geometrical isomerism (G.I.)
blocks.text:
Geometrical isomerism (G.I.): Different configuration due to restricted rotation.

• Alkenes (>C=C<), oximes (>C=N—) and azo compounds [—N=N—] etc.,   show G.I. due to restricted rotation about double bond.

• Cycloalkanes show G.I. due to restricted rotation about single bond in ring.

Condition for Geometrical Isomerism

• Only those alkenes show G. I. in which "Each
$\mathrm{sp}^2$ carbon have different atoms or groups"

• In cycloalkane system; atleast two
$\mathbf{s p}^3$ hybrid atom of ring individually must have different atoms / groups attached to it.

Nomenclature systems of geometrical isomers with configuration

Cis-Trans configuration

If same groups are at same side then cis and if same groups are at different side then trans.

blocks.title: Physical properties of cis and trans alkenes
blocks.text:
• Dipole moment :

Example: But-2-ene

Therefore, cis > trans (Dipole moment).

• Polarity α μ (Dipole moment)

Generally, cis > trans

• Boiling Point (B.P.):

Generally, cis molecule has higher boiling point than trans molecule due to more polarity.

• Melting point:

Melting point depends on packing efficiency.

blocks.title: Calculation of total number of geometrical isomerism
blocks.text:
When compound is unsymmetrical No. of G.I. = $2^{\mathrm{n}}$

When compound is symmetrical No. of G.I. =  $2^{\mathrm{n}-1}+2^{\mathrm{p}-1}$

where  $\mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}$ (when n is  even) and $\mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{n}+1}{2}$ (when n is odd)

where n = no. of restricted rotatory system (double bond) about which G.I. is possible

blocks.title: Conformational isomerism / Rotational isomerism / Conformations
blocks.text:
• The different arrangement of atoms in space that result from the rotation around single bond are called conformations. The phenomenon is called conformational isomerism.
  • Bond length, bond angle are same in all the conformers.
  • These are interconvertible forms of a same compound so there is no change in boiling point, melting point, dipole moment.
  • There are infinite conformations of a compound
  • If there are three continuous single bond present in a compound then it shows conformation.
Conformations of ethane $\left[\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_3\right]$:

In ethane, staggered form is more stable than eclipsed form by 12.5 kJ/mol.

blocks.title: Some Important Terms
blocks.text:
• Dihedral Angle/ Torsional Angle : The angle between two bonds of adjacent atoms.
Dihedral Angle: The dihedral angle in the eclipsed form of ethane is 0°and  in the staggered form is 60°.

  • Types of strain
Conformations of butane:

$\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3$

I (Fully eclipsed form): In this form distance between two methyl groups is minimum so maximum

repulsion or minimum stable. IV (Anti or staggered): In this form distance between two methyl groups is maximum so minimum

repulsion or maximum stability.

III (Gauche form): In this form, the angle between two methyl groups is 60°

Stability order: IV > II > III > I

Energy order: I > III > II > IV

Note: If staggered form is at 60° (in ethane) then it is not gauche form.

Special Cases:

It is not necessary that anti-conformation is always more stable than gauche conformation.

Example:

anti-conformation
